keep: The idea is named in one line up front: an engine turns only part of its heat into work, and every kilowatt of fuel leaves as work or heat carried away.

The picture is the brief's: a fuel band splitting into work, cooling water and exhaust whose widths he drags and which always add back to the fuel; hot and cold sliders in kelvin setting a Carnot line the work stops at, in red; the 60 to 70% band shaded; a generator skin. The first-law cylinder is a still drawing on the screens before it.

Every number is a control, an assumed example, a cited or textbook constant, or computed from a shown rule: 200 kPa × 0.001 m³ = 200 J, 500 − 200 = 300 J, 1 − 300 ÷ 800 = 62.5%, 1,000 − 350 − 300 = 350 kW, 300,000 ÷ 38,500 about 7.8 kg/s.

Each misconception the brief names has a puzzle with its own wrong pick: the signs of Q and W (screens 2 and 4), heat rejected as if it vanished (screen 6's 650 and 700 kW, screen 12's 120 kW), Celsius in the Carnot limit (screen 10's 96%), and the limit moving with effort rather than temperature (screen 10's friction pick). The real-engine limit is taught as debated, not marked wrong.
The mixed puzzles reach back: screen 12 uses efficiency from Mechanics and materials, screen 13 uses lesson 1's flow × specific heat × warming with seawater's 3,850.

The analogy is from his trade, a motor's power balance, reproduces the main result (input = output + heat, always) and breaks at the real point: a heat engine is capped by its temperatures before design starts.
Footnotes sit on words their quotes support, one per sentence. The validator reports no problems.
fix: Causal step skipped, the big one: why an engine must reject heat at all. [^2] is asserted, not explained. Add a 'One way to picture it' step: to go round again the gas must be squeezed back; squeezed hot, it would push back as hard as it pushed out and take back all its work; cooled first, it pushes back less, so the squeeze costs less than the push gave, and that cooling is the heat rejected.

Causal step skipped: the loop's internal energy coming back is stated for a closed gas, then applied to a diesel, which swaps its gas each turn. Bridge it: in steady running nothing builds up inside the engine, so the energy in each second equals the energy out.

Causal step skipped: why kelvin in the Carnot limit and why only temperature moves it. Say it is a ratio of temperatures, and lesson 3 showed a ratio needs true zero; then say a hotter hot side or a colder cold side raises it, and less friction or a bigger engine cannot.

Contested point taught too thinly. The explain says 'debated' but gives neither side nor why both can be read as true. Give both in a sentence each, and say the answer turns on which hot and cold temperatures you choose.

Talks about the idea instead of teaching it: 'the cooler must carry the cooling flow' gives no number. Say the 300 kW the cooler carries is nearly as big as the 350 kW of electrical output, which is why a cooler is sized on the heat rejected, not on the set's rating.
Paragraph 2 carries five ideas (internal energy, the first law, signs, work as area, lock and compression). Split it: the law and its example in one, the area and the signs in the next.
Jargon before it is earned: 'Then 650 kW is rejected' uses 'rejected' unexplained. Say 'heat rejected' means heat carried away, and why the word 'loss' misleads.
Worked example in practice: '400 kW of electrical output from 40% of its fuel' reads badly. Say 'at 40% efficiency, fuel to electrical output'.

Ignores does not say what the Carnot line would wrongly suggest. Add that it assumes all the heat taken in at the hot temperature and all given out at the cold one, and that which two temperatures fit a real diesel is debated, so the sliders leave the choice to him.
The brief's sentence names two changes. Keep one change at its heart: the work stopping at the line while cooling and exhaust take up the rest, so the flows still add to the fuel.
